overview: This 100-page file documents Japanese military intelligence activity in Europe during and immediately after the Second World War, alongside American efforts to identify, exploit, and coordinate intelligence about those operations. Its records range from early-1945 proposals and SHAEF directives for a London-centered Allied collection system to detailed assessments and interrogation-based studies of Japanese networks in France, Switzerland, Sweden, and Finland. Particular attention is given to military attaché Makoto Onodera, the organization and communications of the Stockholm and Helsinki offices, cooperation with European intelligence services and individual sources, espionage directed chiefly against the Soviet Union and Western Allies, and Finnish assistance with cryptanalysis.
interest: The file is especially valuable because it combines policy-level planning for Allied intelligence coordination with unusually granular reconstructions of Japanese personnel, sources, finances, communications, security practices, and collected information. It reveals that Japanese intelligence in Europe depended on a multinational web of Polish, Finnish, Baltic, German, Hungarian, Swedish, and other contacts rather than operating only through formal Axis channels. The source-by-source and target-country summaries, cryptanalytic material, and personnel appendices make the file particularly useful for mapping networks, studying intelligence exchange, and tracing how wartime espionage was investigated during the transition to the postwar period.
